text: Sysmon — System Monitor — is a free tool from the Microsoft Sysinternals suite, originally written by Mark Russinovich and Thomas Garnier. It is not installed on Windows by default; someone has to deliberately download and install it, as a service plus a device driver that watches system activity continuously. It's what you deploy when 'a logon happened' isn't enough, and you need to know what that logon then did.

The Event IDs from Lesson 10 tell you a lot about logons and account changes, but almost nothing about what a process actually did after it started. Windows' native auditing can log that a process was created, but not, by default, the full command line it ran with — and that command line is frequently where an attack reveals itself. A plain powershell.exe is a very different story from one launched with an encoded, obfuscated command. Sysmon closes exactly that gap.

Three event types matter most. Event ID 1, Process Create, logs the full command line, hash, and parent process for every process that starts. Event ID 3, Network Connection, logs source and destination IP and port whenever a process reaches out over the network. Event ID 11, File Create, logs file creation — including when a file's creation timestamp gets overwritten, a trick attackers use to make a file look older than it is.

Sysmon writes to its own log, separate from Security, under Applications and Services Logs, Microsoft, Windows, Sysmon, Operational. It's configured through an XML file of include and exclude rules — without filtering, Sysmon generates an overwhelming volume of events, so most real deployments start from a published community baseline, SwiftOnSecurity's config being the best known, and tune it from there.

Every other lesson in this chapter works with what Windows already logs. Sysmon is the deliberate exception — SOC teams install it because even a well-tuned audit policy leaves process-level and network-level visibility on the table. Next: audit policy itself, and the real trade-off between logging everything and logging too little.
